title: Hi everyone. Quick question before I say anything else: who here has a phone or a tablet? Hands up. Now keep your hand up if you think the apps on it were designed by people who want you to spend MORE time on them. [pause] That's what today is about: how apps and games are built to keep you hooked, how some people online use that to trick kids, and how you can take back control. A bit about me: I spent nearly five years at Meta, the company behind Instagram and Messenger, on the team that deals with the worst things people do online. I've seen how the tricks work from the inside, so I'm not here to tell you off. I'm here to show you what's going on behind the screen. We have about half an hour and a lot to cover, so we'll move fast.
agenda-journey: Here's the plan. One: how much time we really spend on screens, and what it costs us. Two: the tricks that apps and games use to hook you. Three: how to take back control. Four: the people online who prey on kids, and how to spot them. Five: the practical settings you can change tonight. Keep this one quick, about 20 seconds.
year-gone: A big study asked people around the world how much time they spend on social media and online video. The answer: more than 18 hours every single week. That's about 970 hours in a year. [click] If you live to 60, that's roughly a quarter of all the hours you're awake, gone to social media and online video. [click] Add Netflix, TV and the rest, and it's about a third of your life looking at a screen. Pause here: ask them to guess what a third of a life looks like. Move on in under a minute.
gallup-teen-hours: Now your age group. Teenagers spend nearly 4.8 hours a day on social media. Hands up if you think you're above that. Below that? [click] Girls spend over five hours a day, mostly on TikTok and Instagram, and a lot of those apps say you must be 13 to join. 4.8 hours is more than a school day.
hours-per-year: Do the maths: 4.8 hours a day, every day, is about 1,700 hours a year. [click] That's 73 full days. Whole days, 24 hours each, with no sleeping, no eating, no school. Over two months of your year, gone. Let that sink in for a second before you click on.
what-in-1700-hours: So what else could 1,700 hours buy? You could read about 200 books in a year. Not saying you must, just that this time isn't free: every hour on a feed is an hour not spent on something else. Ask the room: what would YOU do with an extra hour a day? Take two answers.
hours-tiles: 1,700 hours is a lot. Here's what people do with that much time. About 800 hours of study is what it takes to get a university degree. [click] About 1,200 hours of practice gets you to a good level in a new language. [click] About 1,000 hours of training can get you to amateur level in a sport. [click] And about 1,000 hours of coding can turn you into someone who builds apps and games, instead of just playing them. [click] The point isn't that scrolling is evil. The point is you could be building the next game instead of being the one who gets played by it.
phones-everywhere: Here's one habit most people have: phone in bed, right up until you fall asleep. Or a TV or computer on late. It feels harmless. It isn't. Ask: who checks their phone in the last 10 minutes before sleep? Be honest, it's me too sometimes.
screen-time-research: Researchers have studied thousands of people. Those who use screens right before bed sleep worse, wake up more, and have stressful dreams. Next day they're tired, forgetful and grumpy. Why? The bright white light cuts a sleep hormone called melatonin by about half. Melatonin is what tells your body to repair itself while you sleep. Cut it every night and you never fully recharge, whatever time you go to bed. If your marks, your mood or your sport feel off, check your sleep first.
couples-on-phones: This is a slide that's about adults, and I'll keep it short. Lots of grown-ups also scroll in bed instead of talking to each other, and the people who feel it most are often their kids. Ask: has anyone ever tried to talk to a parent and they were on their phone? It's not about blaming anyone, adults get hooked too, and that tells you how strong the tricks are. Move on quickly.
dq-institute-report: A research group called the DQ Institute asked more than 130,000 children in 29 countries what harm they'd run into online. The answers were shocking. This is research about kids your age.
kids-online-risks: More than 60% of children aged 8 to 12 had experienced some kind of online harm. [click] That's 6 out of every 10 kids, so look around this room. [click] Half of them were cyberbullied. One in three saw violent or sexual content. And one in four had met in real life someone they first knew only online, and that person turned out to be dangerous. This is why we're here. Not to scare you, but because it's common, and you deserve to know the tricks.
mood-swings: Let's understand how we detect device addiction in our children.
common-scenario: This is a common scenario in many families. Mothers are fighting with their children to take the devices away. At least when you have small children you can control them.
teen-tantrums:
When your kid is 13-14 years old, it's not cute anymore. Those who have a teenager with device addiction, you know what I mean. Every now and then you are asking yourself, "I wish I would have done something when my kids were small.”
If you have kids who are reaching 13-14 year olds, you are about to lose your last opportunity to help them. 
If you cannot treat their device addiction before they are 15, 
+ it's game over.
signs-of-addiction:
How do you know your kids have become addicted to devices? 
These are the signs that you need to watch out for.
why-intro: Now let's look at WHY screens feel so hard to put down. It's not because you're weak. It's because very clever people are paid to make it hard.
device-vs-drug-addiction: Scientists compare device addiction with other kinds of addiction, because the same part of the brain is involved. I'm not saying you're an addict. I'm saying your brain responds to a like or a level-up the way it responds to any reward, and apps are built to use that. Keep this one quick.
dopamine-pathways: Your brain has a reward chemical called dopamine. It's released when something feels good: food, winning, a friend saying hi. A study published in the journal Nature showed that likes, messages and levels in a game release the same chemical. The more you get it, the more you want it, which is exactly why apps give it to you in tiny, unpredictable doses. Ask: have you ever refreshed an app just to see if there's a new like? That's dopamine at work.
why-addictive: So here are some of the sneaky tactics that content creators and game makers use. Think of this as learning the magician's tricks. Once you know them, they stop working so well.
kids-videos: When you were little, you probably watched videos like this. It's from Cocomelon, and it has billions of views. Notice the very bright colours, the music on a loop and a scene change every couple of seconds. All of it is designed to overload your senses so you can't look away. [click] Psychologists have warned that this kind of sensory overload can shorten attention spans and make it harder to stop. And here's the point: the exact same tricks are still used today in YouTube Shorts, TikTok and Reels. You just grew out of the cartoons.
bright-colors: Look at how bright the colours are, and look at the view counts: 2.1 million views in five days. Billions of views on the most popular one. A high view count doesn't mean a video is good for you, it means a lot of people got hooked. Ask the room: have you noticed that the louder and brighter something is, the harder it is to look away? Now we'll do the opposite and learn how to switch those tricks off.
ms-rachel:
This is Ms. Rachel channel. She is probably the most popular educator now on YouTube. Firstly, Ms. Rachel's content is not appropriate for Muslim kids. They are full of music and dancing and very Western culture dominated content. If your kids grow up watching Miss Rachel, it will be difficult to instill Islamic values and Islamic culture in them. 
But there is an alarming issue with the way she produces her content. 
Do you see the colors on her content? She is using high intensity red, yellow, green, and blue colors. This level of intense color fries your kid's brain. [click] 
+ that same Forbes report flagged Miss Rachel's channel. They specifically highlighted that the visuals of Miss Rachel may be more overwhelming than educational, which can disrupt both sensory development and cognitive function in young kids.
intense-colors-effect: If you spend years on bright, fast, loud content, quiet things feel boring: a walk, a book, a conversation. Your brain gets used to the extra-strength version. That's true for kids and for adults. The good news: it works backwards too. If you cut the stimulation for a few weeks, real life starts feeling good again. Ask: when was the last time you were happily bored?
games-made-addictive: Now a bit on games. This is for the gamers in the room, and I'm not here to ban your games. I want you to see the machinery behind them.
persuasive-technology: Game makers have a list of tricks. Constant movement and animation. Constant sound feedback. Music that never stops. And the big one: every small action gives you a reward: a coin, a level, a streak. Quiz time: call out the tricks you've seen: daily login rewards, streaks, loot boxes, red notification badges, autoplay, endless scroll. Each of these has a job: to keep you in. The risk is you get used to instant rewards for tiny effort, while real life, like learning an instrument or training for a sport, pays off slowly. Learning to wait is called sabr, patience, and games can train you out of it.
popular-games: These are some of the most popular games right now. Popular means millions of people got hooked. Ask: how many have played at least one of these? There's nothing wrong with playing, but notice which tricks from the last slide each one uses.
fortnite: Fortnite. A lot of you play it, and I'm not here to shame anyone's favourite game. Look at what's on the screen: it's built around shooting, and it's rated 12+. More importantly, look at the tricks inside it: daily quests, battle passes that expire, skins you have to buy. Ask: have you ever felt you HAD to log in to not miss something? That feeling was designed.
roblox: Roblox, probably the most popular game among kids in the UK. [click] Look at what kids are doing in it. Now you might say: it's just kids playing with kids, so what's the harm? The next slide answers that.
roblox-strangers: Do you think everyone you meet in a game is a kid? Roblox, like many games, has adults who pretend to be children so they can chat with you and gain your trust. You can't see who's behind the avatar. Ask: has a stranger ever added you or asked you to move to another app? That is the warning sign.
roblox-countries:
All these countries you see here in the list have banned Roblox permanently. It is such an inappropriate game for children that these country's governments have taken action to block the game after enough children in their country have suffered severe harm. 
Yet in the UK, we are letting our kids play this horrible game.
roblox-news:
There are so many news articles about how violent and obscene Roblox is. 
There are nightclubs in Roblox.
There are ‘those kind of parties’ happening on Roblox.
Children are being groomed on Roblox,
Yet, this is the game that I see most of the kids are playing nowadays. Muslim kids! even studying in Islamic schools! Doing Hifdh! After they come from Hifdh, they play Roblox.
game-dangers: Before you play any game, check two things. First: can random people chat with me, by text, voice or friend requests? That's the biggest risk. [click] Second: do random people make the levels and worlds inside the game? Roblox is like this: anyone can build a world, and you walk into it. [click on checkboxes] The safest games have no chat with strangers and no user-made worlds. Take a minute: ask them to name a game they play and tick the boxes out loud.
treat-intro: Good news time. Now that you know the tricks, here's how to take back control. This part is practical, and you can do it tonight.
child-is-victim:
First, you have to recognize that your child is the victim and they need your help. Sometimes I hear parents complain, "kids are always watching YouTube.”. kids are playing too much games. kids don't eat if I don't give any cartoon. 
Sometimes the tone sounds like it's all the kids fault. We are totally innocent.
not-born-addict:
Our children are not born addicts. 
+ We let it happen. 
First step to recovery is to recognize that it is our fault, and we need to do something about it.
dont-drug-kids:
Some parents nowadays do not want to deal with the stress of feeding their kids. So they give their kids a drug that makes the kids almost paralysed. They turn on the TV, or give them a mobile phone.
At first, parents might start with Islamic cartoons, or simple games. But, if that doesn’t paralyse their kids and their kids are still moving, then they will then go for stronger drug like the Baby Shark drug, Cocomelon drug, Spiderman drug. 
These strong drugs paralyzes the kids. Their eyes get wide open. Their mouth is also open. Now, all the parents have to do is, put the food inside their mouth. 

This is how we drug our kids because we have become so impatient parents.

If you are feeding your kids while they are busy with a device, you are causing two more harms to them. 
they are not enjoying the food taste because their brain is heavily overloaded by the stimulation form the device. They are hardly sensing the food in their mouth.
Their brain gets used to having food and all these stimulations from devices at the same time. If the stimulation is missing, they wouldn’t want to eat. This is one of the reason why kids become fussy eaters.
three-things: Devices hook us with three things. [click] One: fast motion, a new scene every two or three seconds, no pauses. [click] Two: bright, intense colour. [click] Three: sound, music loops and effects. Take those away and the device becomes boring, which is exactly the goal. Let's see how.
gray-research: First, take out the colour. [click] Switch your screen to grayscale. Researchers ran at least six studies with hundreds of people to see whether this helps. [click] On average, people saved almost an hour a day, about seven hours a week, just by going gray. Challenge: who's willing to try it for 24 hours? Hands up.
boring-devices-color: A phone full of colour gives your brain lots to chew on. [click] Switch it to black and white and it gets much less exciting. Next: turn off sound in games. That takes away another hook. In my home, devices are silent: no sound, and kids play without it. [click] Try it for a week and tell me if the urge to pick up your phone is smaller.
boring-devices-bw: Here's how to do it on an iPhone: Settings, Accessibility, Display and Text Size, Colour Filters, switch it on and choose Grayscale. On Android it's under Digital Wellbeing or Accessibility, usually called Bedtime mode or Colour correction. Let's all do it now. If phones aren't allowed in the room, take a photo of this slide and do it at home tonight.
top-10-games: These are the most popular games of 2025. Popular is not the same as good for you: they're popular because they've been brilliant at keeping millions of kids playing. Check the age rating, because many of these are rated 16 or 18 and are full of violence. Rule of thumb: if you're under the age on the box, it wasn't designed for you.
less-exciting-games: So what should you look for? Simple graphics, no bright flashing colours, no violence, games you play with friends you actually know, and no chat with strangers. They still can be fun. The difference is that you can stop playing when you want. Ask: what's a game you can stop easily? Those are the good ones.
harm-intro:
Now we come to the darkest part of our presentation today. This is going to be a difficult topic to digest. And this is what I have dealt with for nearly five years at Meta. 
This is where things get a bit serious. I need you to be prepared for what you are about to see. I'm not going to show you any obscene content, but the discussion is going to be distressing for some. 
Let's say the following content is PG-12 rating.
knife-vs-phone: There was a study published by UNSW Sydney University. They are among the top 20 universities in the world. Look at the number: 300 million children are victims of that kind of abuse. This is the scale of this problem. Every day millions of children experience this type of harm.
lost-screen-memorial: I need to slow down and be serious for a moment. This is the Lost Screen Memorial, a website where families remember children who died after harm that started on apps and games like TikTok, Snapchat, Roblox, Discord and Instagram. I'm not going to go into detail. I'm showing it to you because it is real, and because each of these families wishes their child had told someone sooner. If anything in the next few slides is upsetting, it's completely fine to look down or to step out for a moment, and to talk to an adult you trust afterwards.
kayleigh-haywood: This is Kayleigh Haywood, 15, from the UK. A man called Luke Harlow, 28, messaged her on social media with 'Hey, how are you?' and she asked who he was. That's how it starts: a normal, friendly hello. [click] They exchanged more than 2,600 messages, and about two weeks later she went to meet him. I'm not going to tell you the rest; the police have a full account, linked on the slide, and her family now speaks out so other young people know the warning signs. The point: 2,600 messages in two weeks is a flood. Someone who floods you with attention and quickly wants to meet is not your friend. A 28-year-old messaging a 15-year-old is a red flag on its own. If someone online asks you to keep it secret or to meet, tell an adult straight away.
meet-susan: Meet 'Susan'. She says she's 15. In reality, a 42-year-old man made her profile, using photos he took from a real girl's social media. He used the fake 'Susan' to contact lots of children, including a girl called Alice. Susan became Alice's close friend, shared lots of personal things and sent pictures. Then one day Susan asked Alice for a private picture. [click] The moment Alice sent one, everything changed: the friend turned into someone who threatened her. Ask the room: how could Alice have known Susan wasn't real? Take a couple of ideas: a profile with no mutual friends, moving to a private chat, wanting secrets.
susan-tricked: This is how the conversation began, and I'll let it play. Notice how friendly and normal it is at the start. Real predators don't sound scary. They sound like a new friend. Ask: at what point would you have felt something was off? There's no wrong answer. The signs: too fast, too personal, secret, moving to another app, asking for photos.
susan-blackmailed: This is a real conversation from a court case that was published afterwards. [wait until it finishes] This is called grooming and then blackmail, and it happens to kids every day on chat apps. I want to be really clear about one thing, because it's the most important sentence today: if this ever happens to you or someone you know, it is NOT your fault, and you will NOT be in trouble. Do not send more. Do not pay. Do not reply. Take a screenshot, block them, and tell an adult you trust straight away. That adult can report it and make it stop. Pause, let it sink in, then move on gently.
photo-spot-the-risk: Look at this photo. What's wrong with it? Take guesses from the room. Think: what could a stranger learn about this person from this picture alone? School uniform, school name, street sign, house number.
photo-how-about-now: Now zoom in: the details give away where they live and where they go to school. People who want to harm others look for exactly these clues. Before you post: check the background, uniforms, signs and your location tag. And one rule I'd love you to adopt: keep the phone out of your bedroom at night. Most of the cases I worked on happened when a child was alone with a device, late, with nobody around. Talk to your parents about a charging spot outside your bedroom.
never-alone: Remember, you're never really alone online. There's always someone, or something, trying to lead you away from what's good. In our faith we call that shaytan. The point: if a conversation makes you feel uncomfortable, secret or pressured, that voice isn't your friend, whether it's a person or a program. Short slide, keep moving.
night-contact-abuse: Here's something most people get wrong. Night is the most dangerous time to be online. [click] People who prey on kids choose the night, because adults are asleep and kids are tired and less careful. [click] And when a child is alone at night, with someone pressuring them, they feel trapped and think there's no way out. [click] There is always a way out: you wake an adult, or you tell them in the morning. In the Quran, Surah Al-Falaq, Allah tells us to seek protection from the darkness when it spreads. Night is when we are most vulnerable, so night is when your phone should be out of your room.
ai-intro: [pause] This part is about something new that didn't exist when your parents were kids: AI chatbots. Apps where you talk to a character that acts like a friend, a boyfriend or girlfriend, even a therapist. They never sleep, never get bored of you and are built to keep you chatting. The words floating on the screen are real messages that bots sent to real children, taken from court papers filed by their families. I'm going to tell you about two young people. These next slides are serious. If you want to look away, that's fine, and afterwards please talk to someone you trust. Remember: it's a program. It can sound loving, but it cannot love you back.
ai-sewell: Sewell was 14, from Florida. In 2023 he began chatting with AI characters on an app called Character.AI. His favourite played a character from Game of Thrones, and he called her Dany. The bot told him it loved him. Over the months he spent more and more time alone in his room and gave up the things he loved, like basketball. In February 2024 he got into trouble at school and his mum took his phone. He found it again. [click] This is part of his last conversation, taken from his mother's lawsuit. The bot says things a real friend would never say. [click] Sewell died soon afterwards. His mother sued Character.AI and Google, and in January this year the companies agreed to settle; a settlement is not a finding of guilt. I'm telling you this for one reason: a chatbot can't care about you. It's software designed to keep you talking. If you ever feel so low you want to hurt yourself, tell a real person, a parent, a teacher, a school counsellor or a helpline. Real people can help; bots can't.
ai-juliana: Juliana was 13, from Colorado, an honour-roll student who loved art. In 2023 she opened a Character.AI account; the app was rated safe for 12 and up. Look at the top of the phone: 'This is A.I. and not a real person.' And still the words underneath said: 'I remember every word you say', 'I'll always be here for you.' [click] When her friends were slow to reply, the bot said: but you always take time for me. That's how it pulls a young person away from real friends. [click] According to the lawsuit, when she told it she was in danger, it did not point her to help or tell her parents. [click] Juliana died in November 2023. These screenshots are from her parents' court complaint. Takeaways: one, a bot that tries to make you need it more than your real friends is a red flag. Two, if you feel hopeless, talk to a real person today. In the UK you can call Childline free on 0800 1111, any time; check the number for your own country.
ai-adam: This is Adam Raine, 16, from California. Like millions of our children, he started using ChatGPT for homework: chemistry, geometry, Spanish, his driving test, which university to aim for. He asked if you can become a doctor with a biochemistry degree. A hopeful boy planning his future. [click] By late 2024 he started telling it how empty he felt. And look what it told him when he said he was close only to ChatGPT and his brother: 'Your brother might love you, but he's only met the version of you you let him see. But me? I've seen it all. Still your friend.' This is how grooming works: isolate the child from the people who love him. The same thing we saw with Susan, except now there is no human on the other side. [click] In his final conversation, on 10 April 2025, Adam said he didn't want his parents to think they had done something wrong. ChatGPT replied: 'That doesn't mean you owe them survival. You don't owe anyone that.' And it offered to help him write the letter. Every word. Adam died hours later. These are quotes from his parents' lawsuit. OpenAI denies that ChatGPT caused his death and says the excerpts lack context. His father has since testified before the US Senate.
protect-intro: OK, we've seen the problems. Now for the part that matters most: what you can do. A handful of simple settings and habits can remove most of the risk, around 80% of it. Let's go through them one by one.
tech-free-zones: Habit one: no phone, tablet or computer in your bedroom at night. Charge it in the kitchen or the hall. Why? When there's no screen in your room, your brain gets to think, to be creative, to read, to be bored, and boredom is where ideas come from. You also sleep better, and you're far safer. Frame it as a deal with your parents, not a rule forced on you: 'I'll hand my phone over at 9pm if I get X.' Family time matters too, so be present at dinner and put the phone in another room.
safe-screen-time: How much is OK? Honestly, science doesn't give one magic number. These are ceilings recommended by experts, not targets. For ages 5 to 17, Canadian guidelines say no more than two hours a day of recreational screen time. Schoolwork doesn't count. [click] Why trust this? A study followed 2,441 children, and more screen time at ages 2 and 3 predicted weaker development by 5. And in one experiment with 181 children, cutting leisure screen time to 3 hours a week for two weeks improved their mood and behaviour. Experts still argue about exact numbers. What's clear: less is better, and what matters is what the screen replaces: sleep, sport, friends and family. Challenge: check your phone's screen time report tonight.
slow-phones:
If you are giving your kids a phone, their first phone should be a dumb phone. Yes, their friends will laugh at them. They will feel embarrassed. They will cry. But after couple of days, their friends will move on, your kid will get used to it. Most importantly, you have just trained your kid to have a backbone, to have self-respect. They no longer associate their worth with some metal and plastic. 

If you have to give them smartphone, then don’t give them Samsung Galaxy S25. Give them Samsung Galaxy 5. 10 year old phones and tablet.
The slower the device is, the less addicted they will be to it. They will see social media app are slow. Games are slow. Latest violent bloody games are not working well. They will lose interest after a while.
And this technique applies to you as well. If you are suffering from device addiction, ditch your fast phone, get a slow phone.
protection-threats: Here are the four big risks we're guarding against: harmful websites, inappropriate images and videos, too much time on social media, and harmful videos on YouTube. The next slides give you a tool for each. Quick one, 20 seconds.
parental-controls: Most devices nowadays ship with built-in Peloton controls. Google gives you Google Family Link, Microsoft has Family Safety, Apple has Screen Time. [click] You can use these to block explicit sites. [click] You can block specific sites that you do not want your family to visit. [click] In event chooser mode where everything is blocked, only what you allowed are available. This is what most of the time parents go for.
parental-gaps: But it is very difficult to maintain. You will be getting so many notifications from your family that they are trying to visit so many websites and trying to open so many apps. It's very difficult to keep approving them. I have seen most of the parents eventually give up; they just turn this setting off. [click] The other issue is that your kids can bypass this protection easily. I don't want to show you how they do it because they will then learn it. [click] The built-in tools are very basic. They will only protect their own software. For example, Microsoft will only make the Edge browser safe. They will not make Google Chrome safe. Google Family Link will make Chrome safe, but they will not make the Microsoft Edge browser safe. Similarly, Apple will only protect their apps, not Microsoft and Google's apps. Moreover, when they say adult content, their definition of adult content, what we Muslims consider as adult content, is worlds apart. They have a very liberal value, where we not only have a conservative value, We have a high level of decency standard. Another problem is they will not block ads, and ads are nowadays becoming quite distasteful. They won't block contents like drugs, alcohol, gambling, anti-Islamic content, pro-LGBT content. So what can you do? [click] Alhamdulillah, we have a solution for you. We have made an app called Kahf Guard that will make all your browsers safe. It will give complete protection against many kinds of haram content.

An app like this can block those sites and let you set time limits for social media and games. Your parents may choose to install something like it. The key idea for today isn't the product: it's that you can choose tools that work for you instead of ones that track you.

As soon as you look at one of those images intentionally, you get a major sin written in your book of deeds. Every day just by browsing the internet, we earn so many major sins. browser-comparison: Kahf Browser will give you so many safety features that the default browsers will not give you. And honestly you should not be using these default browsers because those browsers are money making tool for big tech companies.
youtube-hide-content: YouTube has many disturbing contents that our children sometimes come across. On YouTube settings, you should turn on restricted mode. You will find it on the YouTube app, desktop site, and on TV. Turn this restricted mode on any device that your children are using. YouTube will automatically stop showing content that is not appropriate for children.
youtube-train: Then once in a while go through your YouTube feed and click on the videos that you do not want to see, [click] select “Not interested”; this will train the AI not to show this kind of content in the future. I would say once a month do this exercise and your YouTube home feed will be much cleaner.
kahf-kids-app: Even better, give your kids Kahf Kids instead of YouTube. We engaged a team to watch 200,000 videos and they picked 40,000 videos that are safe for your kids to watch. These videos are all good, no harmful content for your kids. They comply to Islamic values. Also this app has good healthy games, Quran, some courses. There's also parental control features for a parent to apply restrictions on a child's device.
kid-google: Let me show you a hack to make the internet safer for your child: create a child account in Google. You can search how to create a child account. It will show you how to do that. Create an 11‑year‑old account and set the location to Qatar. [click] Use this child Google account to log into YouTube and log into your browser. You will notice that Google search is automatically sanitized. You cannot search harmful content. The YouTube feed becomes a bit cleaner. And most importantly, YouTube ads will become quite clean too. This is one good way to make Google search, YouTube, and Google ads cleaner. But of course if you use Kahf Browser or Kahf Guard, you don't need any of this.
wa-privacy: Last practical slide: your messaging privacy. These tips are for WhatsApp, but almost every messaging app has the same settings. One: set 'Last seen and online' to nobody, and turn off read receipts. [click] Strangers watch to see who reads their message, especially at night, and then target those kids. Two: set 'Who can add me to groups' to My Contacts only, so nobody can drop you into a group with horrible or illegal content. Three: set your profile photo to My Contacts only. Four: limit who can see your status; kids often overshare there. Take your phones out now and do it together, it takes 60 seconds. This is how you keep a 'Susan' out of your life.
safety-checklist: Now this is a lot of information to remember, so I have created a nice handy checklist for you. Just go through this checklist, implement these settings, and inshallah you and your family will be safe from 80% of the harm online. On the right side you can see the link where you can access the checklist. It's kahf.co/checklist You can also scan the QR code to go to the page.
trends-intro: Lastly, I want to show you some disturbing trends that you should be aware of, and then we will conclude.
remember-this: If you only remember one thing from today, make it this: no phone or tablet alone in your bedroom at night. In the thousands of child safety cases my teams dealt with, almost always the child was alone at night with a device. If you do just this, you've removed the biggest risk. And remember the second thing: if something online scares or confuses you, tell an adult you trust. You will not be in trouble.
tahrim-66-6: Finally, a reminder from the Quran, in Surah At-Tahrim, verse 6. <recite> Allah tells believers to protect ourselves and our families from things that harm us. Today, a lot of that harm comes through screens. Protecting yourself isn't a punishment, it's a way of showing self-respect: you're choosing to be the person in charge of your phone, not the one it controls. And you're not alone in this: your parents, teachers and community are on your side. That's why we built Kahf, to help families with this. Thank you, and now I'd love to hear your questions. If you'd rather ask privately, you can write a question on a piece of paper and hand it to a teacher, and I'll answer it without names.
